title: Turkey's Diesel Imports From US and India Hit Records as Russia Ban and Iran War Force Supply Diversification
subhead: Shipping data shows Turkey scrambling for non-Russian diesel barrels after Moscow's export ban and Iran-war disruption, cutting Russia's share of its diesel imports from 85% to 20% in a year. Meanwhile, Kavala presses for release after the Strasbourg ruling and Ankara keeps its restraint on Israel ahead of the October election.

sections.heading: Energy: Turkey Diversifies Diesel Supply at Record Pace
sections.body:
Turkey's imports of diesel from the United States and India hit record levels in August, according to shipping data from commodities firm Kpler, as a Russian export ban and Iran-war disruption force importers to diversify. Kpler data shows Turkey has imported more than 120,000 barrels per day of Indian diesel and 90,000 bpd from the US so far this month — the highest monthly totals on record going back to 2017, Reuters reports.

The shift is stark: Russia's share of Turkey's diesel imports has fallen to 20% in August, down from 85% in 2025, when Russia supplied 281,000 bpd, according to Turkey's energy regulator. Russian diesel imports to Turkey have dropped to around 80,000 bpd in August from above 200,000 bpd earlier this year. Russia banned diesel exports until at least the end of August after Ukrainian strikes on refineries disrupted domestic supply, and industry sources say the ban may extend into September. Middle Eastern supply has also been curbed by war damage to refineries and reduced shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Energy Aspects, which tracks flows separately, estimates India sent a smaller 74,000 bpd and the US 70,000 bpd in August — still the highest since 2022 and 2019 respectively. 'With Russian refinery disruptions and export restrictions, Turkey is having to scramble for barrels from the non-Russian pool,' Sparta Commodities analyst Abhishek Kumar told Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is being forced to rewire a critical energy supply chain in real time — a costly, logistically complex shift that exposes its dependence on Russian fuel and its exposure to both the Ukraine war and the Iran conflict. The diversification is a strategic hedge, but it comes at a price premium and reveals how vulnerable Turkish energy security is to disruptions on two fronts.

sections.heading: Kavala Presses for Release After Strasbourg Ruling
sections.body:
Philanthropist Osman Kavala on Thursday demanded the authorities release him from prison in line with the European Court of Human Rights ruling handed down Tuesday, in a written statement on his website, Reuters reports. Kavala argued the right to liberty must not be restricted without 'convincing and concrete evidence' of a criminal offence, pointing to his acquittal in the 2020 Gezi trial as proof of the lack of evidence.

The Strasbourg court ruled against Turkey on Tuesday, finding Ankara sought to silence Kavala and calling for his immediate release on grounds of serious human rights violations, including that his continued detention amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment. Kavala has been held in Silivri high-security prison near Istanbul since 2017 and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2022 over his role in the 2013 Gezi Park protests. European Parliament rapporteur on Turkey Nacho Sanchez Amor called the ruling 'one of the harshest judgements to have come out of Strasbourg to date,' telling T24 it highlights structural problems in the Turkish judiciary.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the direct test of Ankara's response to Tuesday's ruling — the same case that prompted yesterday's reports that Turkey is floating a reconsideration of its place in Europe's rights system. Whether the government complies, ignores, or retaliates will define the trajectory of Turkey-EU judicial relations and set a precedent for how Ankara handles Strasbourg rulings going forward.

sections.heading: Turkey Holds Restraint on Israel Ahead of October Election
sections.body:
Ankara is likely to maintain its restraint in responding to Israeli strikes on Syria until after Israel's general election in October, as it does not want to hand Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a lifeline in his struggling campaign, Middle East Eye reports, citing Turkish officials. Israeli strikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northern Syria, about 70km from the Turkish border, were seen as provocative but did not surprise Ankara.

Israel claimed Turkey was preparing to deploy air defence systems at the base, a claim Ankara denies — a position supported by statements from Syrian and US officials, per MEE. A regional official told MEE that both sides had previously agreed, in talks in Baku last year, that the area north of the T4 airbase near Palmyra would form a dividing line between Israeli and Turkish security zones in Syria. Ankara views last week's strikes as a violation of that understanding, and Israel's decision not to use the bilateral hotline during the strikes is seen as particularly dangerous. Turkish officials expect the Israeli election to bring a change of government, pointing to opposition from figures including former general Yair Golan to Netanyahu's escalation.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is deliberately absorbing Israeli provocations in Syria rather than escalating, betting on a post-Netanyahu government. The risk is that this restraint is read as weakness by Israel, and that the collapse of the informal deconfliction understanding — including the hotline — raises the odds of a miscalculation near the Turkish border before October.

sections.heading: Mecca Defense Pact Expands as Pakistan Adds Kuwait, Bangladesh Circles
sections.body:
The Mecca defense pact involving Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan continues to institutionalize, with Pakistan signing a new defence cooperation agreement with Kuwait on Thursday, days after joining the Saudi-Turkey military pact, according to Firstpost and Moneycontrol. The Kuwait deal expands cooperation in training, capacity building and border management.

Separately, reports indicate Bangladesh is considering joining the Mecca pact, with sources telling NDTV that conversations on Dhaka's membership came up in discussions. A Jamaat-e-Islami leader said Dhaka's decision should not 'disturb' anyone, per Moneycontrol. Analysts at Outlook India note the pact is only beginning to institutionalise coordination and that the three core members have different threat perceptions.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca pact is quietly broadening its footprint across the Muslim world, with Turkey at its center alongside Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Each new member — Kuwait, potentially Bangladesh — extends a security architecture that runs parallel to, and partly outside, traditional Western alliances, giving Ankara additional leverage in the Gulf and South Asia even as it manages its NATO relationship.

sections.heading: SDF Dissolution Follow-Through and Syrian Unity
sections.body:
Turkey continues to welcome the formal dissolution of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the Syrian army, with the AK Party calling it an important step toward strengthening Syrian unity, Reuters reported Wednesday. Ankara has called for a stable, unified Syria following the dissolution, per Anadolu Agency. The formal dissolution, which has controlled large parts of northern and eastern Syria, has been welcomed by the US and Turkey, though questions remain over Syria's future, the Irish Times reports.

The deal is expected to pave the way for several key decisions in the next phase, including political arrangements, according to reports. Turkey's core demand — that the YPG's military structure be dismantled and not reconstituted under a new name — remains the central test of whether the dissolution is genuine or cosmetic.
sections.whyItMatters: For Ankara, the SDF dissolution is the culmination of years of pressure, but the real question is implementation: whether the YPG's command structure is genuinely folded into Damascus's army or merely rebranded. Turkey's border calculus and its ability to claim a strategic win in Syria depend on what happens on the ground in the coming weeks.

bottomLine: Today's defining development is economic: Turkey is being forced to rebuild its diesel supply chain at record speed, cutting Russia's share from 85% to 20% in a year as Moscow's export ban and the Iran war squeeze supply. It is a costly but strategically significant hedge that exposes both Turkey's energy dependence and its resilience. Politically, Ankara is absorbing Israeli provocations in Syria while betting on a post-Netanyahu Israel, and it faces a direct test over whether to comply with the Strasbourg ruling on Kavala. The Mecca pact's quiet expansion adds a new layer to Turkey's regional positioning. The through-line: Turkey is managing multiple simultaneous pressures — energy, judicial, and military — with a mix of forced adaptation and calculated restraint.
sources: Reuters, Kpler, Energy Aspects, Sparta Commodities, Middle East Eye, Yahoo News, Anadolu Agency, Irish Times, Firstpost, Moneycontrol, Outlook India, NDTV, Jurist, Bianet
